title: Labor votes down bid to block foreign terrorist fighters
text:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  14:27 AEST, 10 September 2026   |  Updated:  14:51 AEST, 10 September 2026

156

View  comments

The Albanese government has voted against a One Nation bill that would have stopped terrorist fighters returning to Australia, sparking a fiery response from Pauline Hanson.

Labor was joined by the Greens and key crossbench senators to vote down the Protecting Australians from Foreign Terrorist Fighters Bill in the Senate on Thursday.

The bill proposed the creation of a court-based foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order.

It would have allowed the Home Affairs Minister to apply to the Federal Court to block the return of Australians found to have voluntarily served, participated in or materially supported a listed terrorist organisation overseas.

The bill also included tougher bail rules for terrorism offenders, expanded passport cancellation powers, and made it a crime to facilitate the return of suspected terrorist fighters.

During the debate, Hanson slammed the Albanese government for failing its 'first responsibility' to keep the country safe.

'The first responsibility of any government is to keep Australians safe,' she told the Senate.

'Australians rightfully expect this government to put their safety and our national security above all else.'

Labor, the Greens and key crossbench senators have voted down a One Nation bill that would have stopped foreign terrorist fighters from returning to Australia, prompting a furious response from party leader Pauline Hanson

Hanson accused the government of enabling the return of women linked to Islamic State and claimed existing laws were too weak to protect the community.

'If the minister genuinely believes the law stops him from keeping Australians safe, his job is not to shrug and accept it. His job and the parliament's job is to come into this place and change it,' she said.

The legislation was primarily driven by One Nation's opposition to the recent return of 19 Australian women and children from Syrian detention camps in May.

The women, dubbed the 'ISIS brides', travelled to Islamic State-controlled territory during the group's rise in Iraq and Syria.

One Nation argued the women willingly supported the terrorist organisation and should be permanently barred from returning to Australia, while the government maintained it is legally required to allow citizens to return under current national security and counter-terrorism laws.

The Albanese government has denied it helped repatriate the group.

Opponents of the bill argued it was unlikely to withstand legal scrutiny and duplicated powers that already exist under Australia's temporary exclusion order regime.

A Senate inquiry earlier this year heard evidence that key provisions were drafted too broadly, with concerns raised about the undefined phrase 'protect the Australian community' and uncertainty around what conduct would trigger a foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order.

The bill would have blocked ISIS fighters from being able to return to Australia (file)

Greens senator David Shoebridge labelled the legislation unconstitutional and accused One Nation of pursuing 'clickbait' politics rather than national security reform.

'They're bringing in a piece of legislation that they know is unconstitutional, they know is going to get struck down by the courts,' he said.

Independent senator David Pocock also opposed the bill, pointing to evidence received during the inquiry process.

'There is a real issue for debate here, how do we as a country deal with Australians returning after making the decision to travel to and in some cases support terrorist organisations,' he said.

'It's a nuanced issue, one where reasonable minds can reach different conclusions.'

No Labor senators spoke during the debate.

After the vote, Hanson took to social media to accuse Labor, the Greens, Fatima Payman and Pocock of putting returning terrorist fighters ahead of the community's safety.

'One Nation's Bill to Protect Australians from Foreign Terrorist Fighters trying to return to the country was voted down this morning in the Senate,' she wrote.

'I regret to inform you Labor, Greens, Senators Payman and Pocock joined together to support returning fighters over the safety of Australians.'

During the debate, Hanson slammed the Albanese government for failing its 'first responsibility' to keep the country safe

Hanson said the government’s refusal to support her bill raised questions about transparency and accountability.

'The government's refusal to make a submission to our inquiry, its failure to produce substantive advice to the Senate, and its willingness to exclude its own officials from secret discussions about returning terrorist sympathisers betray a disturbing disregard for transparency and accountability,' she said.

'Australians are entitled to conclude that their protection has been put second to the Government's desire to return terrorists and their sympathisers to the country.'
